definition: The spot market (a.k.a. cash market) is the market for immediate delivery of a commodity — for energy, this can mean delivery anywhere from about five seconds to one month out — typically involving small-quantity purchases for immediate use.
core_idea: Spot trades involve the physical transfer of a standardized quantity of a commodity for a set price 'on the spot,' analogous to buying fast food or flipping a light switch (immediately buying and consuming electricity); electricity spot trading is limited to parties who can deliver or use power right away.
key_points: 'Immediate' delivery in energy spot markets can span from seconds up to about a month, given the practical complexity of delivering some energy commodities.
Spot market participants are typically consumers buying small quantities for immediate use.
Only parties able to physically deliver or immediately use power can trade in the electricity spot market.
relationships: Contrasted directly with the forward market definition
trading_implications: Spot market access for electricity is inherently restricted to physical delivery/use capability, unlike purely financial markets.
caveats: Thinking 'spot' delivery always means instantaneous (seconds) rather than potentially up to a month for some energy commodities.
